hero.eyebrow: A real home SOC, built and broken on purpose
hero.title: I built a Security Operations Center from a repurposed laptop.
hero.titleHighlight: Then I tried to break it.
hero.subtitle: Wazuh, Suricata, TheHive and Cortex, wired together across 9 real machines — Windows, Linux and macOS — to detect and automatically contain a ransomware-style attack on a simulated media storage network. Every bug on this site is a real bug I hit and fixed.

items.title: Detection
items.text: Wazuh SIEM with File Integrity Monitoring, Sysmon, auditd and 8 independently deployed Suricata network sensors — not a single mirrored tap.

items.title: Automated response
items.text: A custom correlation rule fires a Python Active Response chain: network isolation, workload failover, and a forensic JSON report — all sharing one incident ID, measured at a 3.00s average end-to-end latency.

items.title: Case management
items.text: TheHive receives every level-7+ alert automatically, Cortex enriches observables against VirusTotal and AbuseIPDB, and four case templates standardize the investigation workflow.

items.title: Vulnerability management
items.text: 24 real CVEs triaged one by one — not just scanned — with an explicit fix / mitigate / accept-risk decision and rationale documented for every single one.

story.title: Why this exists
paragraphs: This lab was built as direct preparation for an internship posting titled "Automated Air-Gap and Ransomware Isolation in Media Storage Networks." Instead of studying the topic in the abstract, I built the actual thing: a simulated broadcaster media pipeline (ingest → live → archive → quarantine) on a real Linux host, wired it into a real SIEM, and spent a week finding out exactly where an automated containment system breaks under load.

Nothing here is a mockup or a tutorial screenshot. Every dashboard, every rule ID, every bug described on this site came out of a real terminal, on real hardware, on my own home network. The hardware itself was part of the constraint: an 8-year-old, 2-core laptop repurposed as the SIEM server — which turned out to be one of the most instructive limitations in the whole project.

warstories.title: A few bugs worth reading about
warstories.subtitle: Every one of these was found by testing, not by design review.

items.title: 300 alerts, only 100 forensic reports
items.text: Simulating a mass ransomware event (100 files renamed at once) revealed that my incident IDs — generated with 1-second timestamp resolution — collided under load, silently overwriting forensic evidence. Exactly the moment it would matter most in a real attack.

items.title: A scan that should have been invisible... and was
items.text: A live nmap scan against one of my own machines produced zero alerts anywhere. Turned out to be two separate problems layered on top of each other: a loopback-routing false alarm, and a genuine architectural blind spot in single-sensor Suricata deployments.

items.title: A script that ran and did nothing
items.text: An Active Response script logged 'command dispatched' but never isolated anything. The bug: a big paste in nano had silently deleted the trailing `if __name__ == "__main__":` block. Exit code 0, zero log lines — the signature of a script that only defines functions and never calls them.
